hook.text: In 1700s England, Parliament let landowners fence off shared fields. Millions of peasants lost access.

buildup.text: Open fields were divided, hedged, and consolidated into private farms owned by gentry.

discovery.text: Private ownership allowed experimentation. Enclosed farms could try new crops and methods freely.

twist.text: Displaced rural workers flooded into cities. They became the labor force for the Industrial Revolution.

climax.text: Enclosure boosted food production but destroyed a way of life. Progress came at a brutal human cost.

punchline.text: Fencing the land fed more people—and uprooted millions.

quiz.question: What was the major social consequence of the Enclosure Movement?
options: Displaced rural workers migrated to cities, fueling industrialization

details.summary: The enclosure movement consolidated medieval Europe's open common fields into privately owned, fenced farms. This topic covers how enclosure boosted agricultural efficiency but dispossessed millions of rural poor, driving migration to industrial cities.
details.whyItMatters: Enclosure created the modern concept of private agricultural land. Its social costs—mass displacement and rural poverty—fueled the Industrial Revolution's labor force and shaped debates about land rights that continue today.
takeaways: Enclosure replaced communal strip farming with private, fenced fields
Larger enclosed farms adopted new technologies and rotation systems more easily
Millions of dispossessed rural workers migrated to cities, providing factory labor

faq.question: What was the enclosure movement?
faq.answer: Enclosure was the process of consolidating scattered communal farming strips and common grazing land into larger, privately owned and fenced farms. In England, parliamentary acts in the 18th and 19th centuries accelerated enclosure dramatically.

faq.question: What were the social consequences of enclosure?
faq.answer: Enclosure displaced millions of small farmers and landless laborers who depended on common land for grazing, fuel, and subsistence. Many migrated to industrial cities as factory workers, while rural poverty and social unrest increased.
